title: Rootstock suckers — shoots from below the bud union

common.applies_to: Established grafted Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or provisional Grandiflora rose (passed PKR-SGT-000003). Any season (Founder decision D1(b)); PKR-SGT-000002 applies. Dormant session: point of origin only. Growing season: supporting signs may be added.
common.preserved_uncertainty: No source describes recognising a sucker on a dormant, leafless rose other than by where it starts (AF-10, Low). Sources disagree on how dependable leaf clues are (C-2), and rootstocks differ by country (AF-9; New Zealand mainly uses *Rosa multiflora* or strains of it), so Pip gives no rootstock-specific cues (R-3 default). One source says a rootstock stub left above the union can also sucker (AF-14, Low; C-6); this isn't used to classify shoots. No source gives a prickle or cane rule (AF-8). No source says what a photo can establish (R-2). Sources are UK, US, Australian and New Zealand.

content.look_for: Let's check for suckers. A sucker is a shoot from the rootstock your rose was grafted onto, below the bud union — the knobbly join near the base. It isn't your rose's own new cane.

criteria.text: Where the shoot starts is the deciding check: below the bud union is a sucker; at the union or just above it is your rose's own new cane, which you keep.
A sucker can start below the soil, sometimes a little away from the plant.
Planting depth varies, so the bud union may be above, at or below the soil.

content.photo_limit: A photo can't show where a shoot starts, especially under the soil. I never decide a shoot is a sucker from a photo.
content.confirm_question: Follow the shoot down with your fingers. Does it start below the bud union, or at or above it?
content.doesnt_match_label: At or above the bud union
content.doesnt_match_note: That's your rose's own new cane. Keep it — the rose's own basal canes are valuable. It's considered in the framework step.
content.not_sure_guidance: That's alright. It's easy to confuse these, even for experienced gardeners. Look again at where the shoot starts, on the plant, not in a photo.
content.any_more_question: Can you see any more shoots like this coming from the base?

sucker_steps.hasShoot: Is there a shoot coming from the base of your rose, or from the ground near it?
sucker_steps.unionVisible: Can you see the bud union — the knobbly join near the base where your rose was grafted?
sucker_steps.noUnion: Then I won't call it a sucker. The union may just be buried. If you like, gently clear a little soil and look again — otherwise leave the shoot, and ask experienced local help if you're concerned.
sucker_steps.ownRoot: If you know your rose grows on its own roots (it wasn't grafted), shoots from the base are the same rose, so none is a sucker — keep them.
sucker_steps.supporting: In the growing season only, these can help you look, but never decide on their own: sucker leaves are often paler or smaller or have a different number of leaflets (though the "seven leaflets" rule isn't reliable); sucker flowers differ from your rose's; suckers are often unusually vigorous, straight and tall.
